name: Eyebrow transplant

lead: An eyebrow transplant moves individual hair follicles into the brow to thicken sparse brows, fill gaps or reshape them, giving the eyes a fuller, more defined frame. Surgeons describe the brow as small but demanding, because angle, direction, density and curl must match the natural pattern.

A 2021 case series of 36 patients using the long-hair follicular unit excision technique reported patient and surgeon scores of 4.7 and 4.3 out of five, and a 2024 study of 81 patients using hair from around the ear reported no significant complications over 15 months. No controlled trials exist.

paras: Follicular units are taken from the scalp or the area behind the ear and placed in small recipient sites angled to follow the brow. Long-hair extraction lets the surgeon see curl to match it. Grafts grow in over months.

Reported series describe few complications, but they are small and surgeon-authored. Mismatched curl, direction or density can look unnatural, and reviews describe corrective operations after unsatisfactory work.

angle.text: Eyebrow transplants thicken sparse brows or reshape them for a fuller, more defined eye frame, visible once grafts grow in. Small surgeon series report high satisfaction, and no controlled trials exist.

lead: Eyebrow transplantation is a surgical hair-restoration procedure in which individual hair follicles, usually taken from the scalp, are placed into the eyebrow to add density, fill gaps or reshape the brow.[1][2] Patients and surgeons describe the result as a lasting alternative to pencil, powder, tinting or semi-permanent tattooing; the transplanted hairs keep growing and need occasional trimming.[3][4] Eyebrows frame the eyes and carry much of the face's expression, so even small changes in their thickness, tail length or tilt change how a face reads.[5]

People seek the operation for several reasons: thinning from over-plucking or genetics, scarring from burns or trauma, medical hair loss, or a wish for a fuller or differently shaped brow.[3][2] Reviews describe follicular unit extraction (FUE) as the most popular technique, and surgeons stress that the brow is small but unforgiving: angle, direction, density and hair curl must all match the natural pattern.[2][6] In looksmaxxing forums, brow transplants appear in plans to thicken or lengthen the brows, change their tilt or lower a high-set brow, usually alongside other procedures.[7][8]

The published evidence consists of surgeon-authored case series, comparative retrospective studies and reviews rather than controlled trials. They report high satisfaction and few complications, and they also document unsatisfactory results that need correction and, in patients with some scarring alopecias, gradual loss of grafts over several years.[9][10][2][2]
infobox: Follicular unit extraction (FUE); long-hair FUE; follicular unit transplantation (FUT)[2][6][10]
Scalp (occipital); periauricular hair; frontal-temporal triangle area; occasionally body hair[9][2][3]

paras: Eyebrow restoration covers non-surgical methods (camouflage, microblading, tattooing and cosmetic prosthetics) and surgical methods that move hair or skin.[3] Wikipedia describes the surgical options as follicular unit transplantation (FUT, in which a donor strip is dissected into single follicular units), follicular unit extraction (FUE, in which units are harvested one by one and leave smaller scattered donor marks), single-hair follicle transplantation for scars where precise angle and density matter, and flaps or full-thickness grafts for larger defects.[3]

Planning involves the donor site (the back of the scalp is typical, with body hair an option that has different texture and growth cycles), the brow shape and hair direction, which surgeons often draw with the patient seated, the quality of the recipient skin, and the number of grafts, commonly 50 to 250 per eyebrow according to Wikipedia.[3] Adjuncts such as fat grafting, PRP or microneedling may be used to improve scarred recipient skin.[3][2]

sections.h: Causes of eyebrow loss and why people seek transplants
paras: Eyebrow thinning or loss, called madarosis, can follow trauma, burns, scarring, genetic predisposition, ageing, over-plucking, hormonal changes and a range of dermatologic or systemic conditions.[3][2] A 2023 review notes that loss of eyebrows and eyelashes affects function and also well-being and quality of life, and that identifying the cause is essential before choosing treatment.[2]

A 2018 systematic review of eyebrow and eyelash transplantation covered 67 articles and 354 patients from 18 countries; most patients were women with a mean age of 29, burns were the most common reason for surgery (57.6 percent of cases), and FUT was the most frequently used technique, with composite grafts and flaps also used and few complications reported.[2] A 2019 review described a sharp rise in demand for facial hair restoration, with women mainly seeking denser brows and men mainly seeking fuller beards.[2]

The wider cosmetic context matters to the demand: Wikipedia's article on eyebrows notes that brow shape has followed fashion, from the shaved and re-drawn brows of eighth-century Japan, to the thin plucked brows of the 1920s and 1930s, to the thick brows associated with Audrey Hepburn, and lists transplantation as an option for people with genetically thin brows or over-tweezed brows.[5] Surgeons have also begun to publish quantitative design data: a 2025 study of 1,482 East Asian participants (1,043 men, 439 women) measured brow morphology and surveyed 513 people on preferences, finding men most often preferred a straight triangular brow and women a smooth arched brow, with an ideal peak at or beyond the outer corner of the eye.[2]

A 2017 review describes the eyebrow as a prominent feature that requires precision in anatomy, design, extraction and implantation, and identifies FUE as the most popular technique.[6] Long-hair FUE, in which hairs are left uncut at harvest so the surgeon can see their curl and length, is described as crucial for matching eyebrow hair because curl and direction must be reproduced; the long hair can also camouflage the recipient area. A study of 134 long-hair FUE patients, 34 of them eyebrow cases, reported a mean of 292 grafts per eyebrow transplant.[11]

Donor choice affects growth rate and texture. A 2024 study used periauricular hair, which has a slow growth rate and fine caliber similar to eyebrow hair,[9] while a 2022 comparison of 155 patients found that hair from the frontal-temporal triangle area (near the temple hairline) grew more slowly than occipital or periauricular hair, was trimmed less often by patients and was associated with a higher proportion of very satisfied patients.[2] Surgeons have also published designs for planning brow shape before surgery: a 2025 prospective study of Chinese men compared a five-point design method (21 patients) with conventional transplantation (33 patients), and blinded raters scored 95.2 percent versus 84.9 percent as improved on the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale.[2]
Surgeons train on models, and a 2023 study described silicone simulation products for learning brow design and planting.[12]

Per Wikipedia, transplanted hairs shed in the first weeks, visible regrowth begins at around three to four months, and near-full results appear by eight to twelve months; graft survival is often reported at above 70 to 80 percent, and the hairs keep growing and need trimming.[3] The 36-patient long-hair series reported natural results in all patients at follow-up, with no asymmetry or folliculitis.[10] In the 81-patient periauricular series, mean surgery time was about 194 minutes for women and 229 minutes for men.[9]
No controlled trials have been published. The human data are case series and retrospective comparisons, usually written by the performing surgeons.

A 2021 case series of 36 patients treated with long-hair follicular unit excision reported natural results with patient and surgeon satisfaction scores of 4.7 and 4.3 out of 5; twelve patients had had unsatisfactory brow surgery elsewhere and four had touch-ups.[10] A separate 2021 series of 134 long-hair FUE patients included 34 eyebrow cases.[11] A 2024 retrospective study of 81 patients (72 women, 9 men) using periauricular hair reported no significant complications over 15 months of follow-up.[9]

A 2022 series of 18 patients with scarred brows from trauma, giant-nevus excision or burns used an atraumatic FUE technique with adjuncts including PRP, microneedling, steroid injections and fat grafting, and reported satisfactory orientation and symmetry, increased self-confidence and no recipient or donor-site complications; its authors proposed atraumatic FUE as a first option for cicatricial brow loss after proper evaluation.[2] A registered trial of FUE for alopecic scars is not specific to eyebrows.[13]

Studies also document problems. A 2024 retrospective review of 100 dissatisfied patients (2011-2021) found sparse brows in 36 percent, uneven density with disordered growth direction in 41 percent, no single-hair grafting in 11 percent, poor blending with the existing brow in 7 percent and mismatched hair characteristics in 5 percent; the authors attributed these to low hair survival, limited understanding of natural brow appearance and poor communication.[2] In ten patients with frontal fibrosing alopecia, a scarring hair-loss condition, 80 percent had excellent growth at 6 to 12 months, but most began losing transplanted hair after three to four years and only one kept all grafts beyond four years; the authors advised warning such patients about likely long-term graft loss.[2]

Microblading deposits pigment in the upper dermis with a hand tool to draw hair-like strokes; it fades faster than machine tattooing, with results lasting up to about two years and touch-ups suggested after roughly six weeks and then every 12 to 18 months.[4] Wikipedia lists misplaced or migrating pigment, colour change and, as with any tattoo, a risk of bloodborne infection among its reported problems, and notes that microblading is not federally regulated in the United States.[4]

Other approaches include tinting, brow powders and gels, botulinum toxin to raise the brow, and surgical brow lifts.[5] Transplants differ from these in using living hair; surgeons who combine them with PRP or microneedling describe doing so to improve recipient skin.[2]

Wikipedia's list of surgical risks includes donor-site problems, unnatural hair direction, asymmetry, graft failure, infection and visible scarring.[3] The published case series report few complications, but are small and written by the surgeons who performed the operations.[9][10] A review of corrective cases describes dissatisfaction after poorly designed or poorly matched grafting.[2] Hair transplantation in general is associated with temporary thinning ('shock loss').[14]
Costs vary widely by country and graft count; Wikipedia's article on hair transplantation reports average per-graft prices from about US$1.07 in Turkey to US$7.00 in Canada for scalp work.[14]

Looksmax.org members mention eyebrow transplants in two ways. One poster asked for a rough price for an eyebrow transplant combined with rhinoplasty and double-jaw surgery, accepting a cheaper foreign surgeon but wanting quality, and was told a consultation would be needed for an estimate.[7] Another laid out a 'morph' plan listing a lowered brow, a longer and more positively tilted brow, a hairline change and facial hair; he asked whether a transplant placed slightly lower would be less risky than botulinum toxin plus eyelid surgery for a lower brow position.[8]

The community's interest follows its general focus on eye-area geometry, where brow position, tilt and thickness are discussed as parts of how the upper face looks, and transplantation is raised as an option alongside makeup, tinting and, for brow position, surgical lifts or botulinum toxin.

lore.intro: Eyebrow transplants come up on looksmax.org as one option within larger plans for brow shape, thickness, length and tilt, and in price questions for combined surgeries.[7][8]

claims.claim: An eyebrow transplant can make brows thicker, longer or reshaped
A transplant could be a lower-risk way to lower the brow than surgery or botulinum toxin

Transplants are for women with over-plucked or thin brows and also for men seeking fuller brows

timeline.event: Japanese court practice of hikimayu: brows shaved or plucked and painted higher on the forehead, an early example of brow reshaping.[5]
Japanese surgeon Okuda describes small hair grafts used mainly for eyebrows and eyelashes.[14]
Cosmetic eyebrow tattooing grows in the US and parts of Asia as an alternative to relying on makeup.[4]
Review summarises hair transplantation to eyebrows, beard, sideburns and eyelashes.[1]
Review of eyebrow transplantation by FUE describes it as the most popular technique.[6]
Systematic review covers 67 articles and 354 patients with eyebrow or eyelash transplantation.[2]
Series of 10 frontal fibrosing alopecia patients reports good early growth but frequent graft loss after 3-4 years.[2]
Long-hair FUE series of 36 eyebrow patients published.[10]
Comparative study of 155 patients tests frontal-temporal triangle hair against periauricular and occipital hair.[2]
Review on managing loss of eyebrows and eyelashes published; silicone training models described.[2][12]
Periauricular-hair series of 81 patients and a review of 100 poor transplants are published.[9][2]
